title: State of Markets II | Andreessen Horowitz
gist: a16z's David George argues tech is now 'the everything cycle', contributing ~76% of S&P 500 earnings growth in 2026, with market leadership rotating from software to hardware/infrastructure as hyperscaler FCF (and increasingly debt) funds the AI buildout. GPU rental rates, even for A100s, are holding or rising despite obsolescence fears while AI adoption remains shallow, and the SaaS sell-off is framed as a growth-driven 'prove-it' re-rating rather than an apocalypse.

insights.claim: Tech contributed roughly 76% of the S&P 500's total earnings growth in 2026 (as of late August), making it the index's earnings growth story since 2023.
insights.speaker: David George
insights.so_what: Index-level earnings growth is highly concentrated in tech; non-tech earnings momentum is weak, raising concentration risk.
insights.quote: contributing ~76% of the SP500’s total earnings growth in 2026 (as of late August)
insights.locator: Tech has steadily compounded earnings growth

insights.claim: Tech should no longer be thought of as a sector: it has replaced durable goods (houses, dishwashers, cars) as the driver of the economic cycle.
insights.speaker: David George
insights.so_what: Macro cycle analysis should treat tech capex and earnings as the core cyclical driver, not housing/durables.
insights.quote: Tech is the everything cycle, now.
insights.locator: What lies beneath that earnings growth

insights.claim: Post-GFC, tech won capital markets because it offered high growth, capital-light models and massive embedded operating leverage from untapped TAM and software's near-zero marginal cost; skeptics of loss-making techcos missed the decade's theme.
insights.speaker: David George
insights.so_what: Historical lesson: betting against loss-making firms with operating leverage on large TAM was costly last cycle.
insights.quote: tech offered massive embedded operating leverage, given substantially untapped TAM, and software’s near-zero marginal cost
insights.locator: As a force in capital markets

insights.claim: The theme of 2026 within tech has been a rotation from software to hardware, with hardware and infrastructure becoming the market's favorites after years of trailing software.
insights.speaker: David George
insights.so_what: Leadership has shifted to semis, power, networking and infrastructure; software is no longer the default tech overweight.
insights.quote: the theme of the year (and beyond), has been the rotation from bits to atoms
insights.locator: Within tech, the theme of the year

insights.claim: The AI buildout is functionally converting hyperscaler free cash flow into semiconductor free cash flow, boosting traditionally sleepy, cyclical, capital-intensive industries like semiconductors, power and networking.
insights.speaker: David George
insights.so_what: Semis/power/networking profits are a direct derivative of hyperscaler capex budgets; watch hyperscaler FCF and capex guidance.
insights.quote: functionally converting hyperscaler free cashflow into semiconductor free cashflow
insights.locator: The AI buildout has caused a surge

insights.claim: AI infrastructure spending is increasingly funded by debt rather than only by hyperscaler profits.
insights.speaker: David George
insights.so_what: Rising leverage in the AI buildout introduces credit-cycle sensitivity and potential fragility to the capex boom.
insights.quote: but increasingly by debt, as well
insights.locator: The AI buildout has caused a surge

insights.claim: The revival of physical industries extends beyond AI: trillions in global infrastructure needs, rising defense spending, grid electrification, manufacturing reshoring, and incoming robots and robotaxis all support it.
insights.speaker: David George
insights.so_what: Multiple independent demand drivers make the atoms trade less dependent on AI alone.
insights.quote: Global infrastructure needs are measured in trillions, defense spending is rising, grids are grappling with the electrification of everything
insights.locator: It’s not just AI that’s

insights.claim: Public and private equity are funding innovation in compute, memory, power, robotics, manufacturing and defense at an intensity not seen in decades.
insights.speaker: David George
insights.so_what: Capital flood into hard-tech categories may compress future returns but signals sustained funding availability.
insights.quote: with an intensity we haven’t seen in decades (if not longer)
insights.locator: In all events, hardware and infrastructure

insights.claim: Demand for compute is still outpacing supply in 2026.
insights.speaker: David George
insights.so_what: Supply-constrained compute supports pricing power for GPU vendors and cloud/neocloud lessors.
insights.quote: demand for compute is still outpacing supply
insights.locator: On the subject of all that capex

insights.claim: Contrary to the bear case that GPUs become obsolete in 3-4 years, GPU rental rates (and thus residual values) have not declined; even the older Nvidia A100 is pricing at or above its level at the start of the year.
insights.speaker: David George
insights.so_what: Undercuts the depreciation-schedule bear thesis on AI capex and supports GPU-backed lending and neocloud economics.
insights.quote: Even the A100 is pricing at-or-above what it was at the beginning of the year.
insights.locator: Rental rates (and thereby residual values

insights.claim: Cheaper intelligence is increasing total compute demand (a Jevons-style dynamic), pushing pricing up for the latest chips while keeping older chips valuable.
insights.speaker: David George
insights.so_what: Falling AI unit costs are demand-expansionary, not deflationary, for compute owners.
insights.quote: As intelligence gets cheaper, demand for compute is only rising
insights.locator: Rental rates (and thereby residual values

insights.claim: Neither compute nor model advancement has been zero-sum so far: both older chips and older models retain substantial value beyond the bears' assumed expiration dates.
insights.speaker: David George
insights.so_what: Value accrues across the AI stack rather than being wiped out by each new generation.
insights.quote: neither compute nor model advancements have been a zero-sum game
insights.locator: The story is far from over

insights.claim: Nearly 30% of S&P 500 companies report some quantifiable impact from AI, but only about 2% report any tracked metric.
insights.speaker: David George
insights.so_what: Enterprise AI adoption is broad but shallow, implying a long runway of deeper (and more spend-intensive) deployment.
insights.quote: only ~2% are reporting any tracked metric
insights.locator: While nearly 30% of SP500 companies

insights.claim: Only a tiny share of users are meaningfully deploying AI agents at any scale.
insights.speaker: David George
insights.so_what: Agentic workloads, which are compute-heavy, remain largely ahead of us.
insights.quote: a tiny share of the overall userbase is meaningfully deploying agents with any scale
insights.locator: While nearly 30% of SP500 companies

insights.claim: As of April 2026, only about 2% of US households were paying for any AI service, though the share is growing.
insights.speaker: David George
insights.so_what: Consumer AI monetization is in its infancy; paid penetration upside is large.
insights.quote: barely ~2% of US households were paying for some AI service
insights.locator: As of April, barely ~2%

insights.claim: GPUs are already running hot even though AI adoption and utilization are at a very early stage, implying substantial further compute demand as adoption matures.
insights.speaker: David George
insights.so_what: Bullish read-through for compute demand durability despite capex-bubble worries.
insights.quote: GPUs are already running hot, even while the data indicates that it’s still so early
insights.locator: The point is that GPUs

insights.claim: The 2026 software sell-off was a discerning re-rating rather than an apocalypse, and AI disruption fears were only one of its causes.
insights.speaker: David George
insights.so_what: Indiscriminate SaaS selling may have mispriced fast growers; dispersion favors stock-picking.
insights.quote: There’s been no apocalypse for software, but there has definitely been a “prove it.”
insights.locator: There’s been no apocalypse

insights.claim: Since ZIRP ended, software inverted from mostly high-growth/unprofitable in 2022 to about 75% profitable but only about 30% growing 20%+ in 2026.
insights.speaker: David George
insights.so_what: Sector multiples compressed because growth slowed, a structural rather than purely AI-driven derating.
insights.quote: ~75% are profitable, but only ~30% are growing 20%+
insights.locator: Since the end of ZIRP

insights.claim: Higher interest rates pushed companies to trade growth for profitability, and slower growth eventually caught up with software multiples.
insights.speaker: David George
insights.so_what: Rate regime drives software valuation; slower-growth SaaS should not expect a return to premium multiples.
insights.quote: slower-growth companies do not beget high-growth multiples, at least not for long
insights.locator: It makes sense, insofar as higher

insights.claim: Fast-growing software companies still trade at multiples in line with historical averages (though below ZIRP peaks); the sector repriced because there are fewer of them.
insights.speaker: David George
insights.so_what: Growth remains rewarded; scarcity of 20%+ growers makes them potential premium assets.
insights.quote: Fast-growing companies are still trading at multiples in line with historical averages
insights.locator: Not for everyone, of course

insights.claim: a16z expects AI to expand the surface area of demand, deepening enterprise and consumer adoption and pushing into new frontiers in robotics, biotech, health and autonomous driving.
insights.speaker: David George
insights.so_what: Positions for AI-enabled growth in robotics, bio/health and AD as next demand frontiers.
insights.quote: We expect that AI will expand the surface area of demand.
insights.locator: We expect that AI will expand

insights.claim: Because the technology is improving at an exponential pace, the author is confident this cycle will not resemble any previous cycle.
insights.speaker: David George
insights.so_what: Signals a16z's stance against applying historical bubble analogies to the AI cycle.
insights.quote: we’re pretty confident that this cycle isn’t going to be like any previous cycle
insights.locator: In general, the technology is improving
